title: Axon projection density did not predict rate or direction of fast spike coupling between six mouse visual areas in two Allen Neuropixels data sets; target preference matched in one data set
abstract: Question: does mesoscale axon projection strength between mouse visual areas predict how often unit pairs in those areas show fast directed spike coupling? We used two Allen Neuropixels data sets: Visual Coding (VC; 50 mice; 3.38 million directed tests; 3,400 links) and Visual Behavior (VBN; 34 mice, 62 sessions; 4.84 million tests; 23,158 links). A link is a significant 1-7 ms lead in the cross-correlogram of two units on different probes in different areas (V1, LM, RL, AL, PM, AM). A binomial model gave one adjusted link log-odds per directed area pair, with control of firing rates and unit distance. We compared these 30 values with two anatomical estimates: the Knox 2019 voxel-model matrix and medians of Allen tracer experiments. The functional profiles agreed between VC and VBN (r = 0.75). The three pre-specified tests failed in both data sets and with both anatomical estimates. Projection density did not predict directed link rate (r = -0.20 to 0.24; area-label permutation p >= 0.44). The anatomical asymmetry between two areas did not predict link direction (r = -0.18 to -0.04). Links went mostly from the lower to the higher area in the hierarchy (VC +1.03, VBN +0.59 log-odds). A strong source-area effect dominated the functional matrix: out-coupling fell with hierarchy rank (Spearman -0.89 VC, -0.83 VBN), but it did not follow anatomical output density. Exploratory analyses added after the first results: within each source area, targets with more axon density had more links in VC (r = 0.62, p = 0.008; experiment medians r = 0.52, p = 0.043), but not significantly in VBN (r = 0.22-0.25, p >= 0.38). The VBN result became significant only with an added area-distance control. Limitations: only 6 areas, so area-level power is low; tracer weights come from other mice; link calls depend on spike counts and on the CCG rule.

display.caption: Left: Pearson r between log10 anatomical weight and adjusted link log-odds for raw values and for the components of an additive source + target decomposition (30 directed area pairs). Bars are 95% intervals from a mouse bootstrap of the functional data (300 refits). They do not include anatomical uncertainty or the small number of areas. Right: per-mouse r (Knox weights) for raw and source-centred values.

Adjusted link log-odds against log10 Knox weight for 30 directed area pairs. Left: raw values (no relation). Right: values after removal of each source-area mean (target preference). Colours give the source area; labels give the target. p values are from the exact area-label permutation (720 permutations).

Directed matrices. Left: log10 normalized connection density from the Knox 2019 voxel model. Middle and right: adjusted link log-odds in VC and VBN. Rows are source areas and columns are target areas. V1 has the lowest anatomical output density but the highest functional out-coupling.
